### Related questions
    - ###### ### What is the purpose of the FINREP? The Financial Reporting Framework (FRF) is a set of rules and guidance developed by the European Banking Authority (EBA) to ensure that institutions report consistent information to the European Central Bank (ECB), which then publishes it in a consolidated format. This allows the ECB to monitor the health of the banking sector across Europe. The FRF consists of two main parts: the Common Reporting Framework (CRF) and the Financial Reporting Framework (FINREP). The CRF provides a common framework for banks to report their data to the ECB. It includes templates for reporting on capital adequacy, liquidity, risk exposure, and other key metrics. The FINREP is a more detailed reporting framework that covers additional areas such as credit risk, market risk, operational risk, and income statement. Both frameworks are designed to provide a comprehensive picture of the financial health of the banking sector and help regulators identify potential risks and vulnerabilities.

question: Article 34(3) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) (same wording with 24(3) of the Banking Consolidation Directive) states that "Paragraphs 1 and 2 shall apply accordingly to subsidiaries of a financial institution as referred to in the first subparagraph of paragraph 1". We are trying to understand what this para. 34 (3) means. Let us assume that there is a financial institution (Institution A), as defined in point (26) of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 CRR, which is not “a subsidiary of a credit institution or the jointly owned subsidiary of two or more credit institutions”. That financial institution then has a subsidiary (Institution B) that is itself a financial institution within the meaning of point (26) of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013. Would that subsidiary (Institution B) be able to passport itself into another member state, per the provisions of Article 34(3)?
ground_truth: The right to carry out relevant activities in other Member States, either by establishing a branch or by providing services, is under the Directive 2013/36/EC provided to a financial institution and its subsidiaries, if that financial institution is a subsidiary of a credit institution or is jointly held by two or more credit institutions and all conditions referred to in Article 34 of that Directive are met. Hence, financial institutions (and their subsidiaries) which are not subsidiaries of credit institutions or jointly held by two or more credit institutions do not fall under the scope of Article 34.

meta.subject_matter: Passporting for financial institutions

baseline.text:
The answer to this question can be found in the CRD IV recitals:

Recital 19 states that the scope of the CRD IV should include all financial institutions, including those that are not credit institutions but are supervised by the competent authorities of their home Member State under the CRD IV. This includes investment firms, insurance undertakings, pension funds, collective investment undertakings, and other entities that provide similar services. The CRD IV also applies to branches of such financial institutions established in another Member State.

Recital 20 states that the CRD IV does not apply to certain types of financial institutions, such as central banks, public sector bodies, and certain types of insurance companies. However, it does apply to branches of these institutions if they are established in another Member State.

Based on these recitals, we can conclude that the CRD IV applies to both Institution A and its subsidiary Institution B. Therefore, Institution B would be able to passport itself into another Member State under the provisions of Article 34(3).

This answer was provided by the European Banking Authority (EBA).

question:
Should a surplus above overcollateralization (above contractual amounts/percentages and also above what rating agencies require to maintain the rating) within a covered bond programme be considered as encumbered, when release and re-assignment of any security requires a signature from external parties (incl. the trustee for the covered bond programme) based on the programme documentation?
If the required signature before withdrawal should still be seen as resulting in encumbrance, also in the case of the situation described below, would it then be relevant, if the Trustee contractually would not be able to say ‘No’ if the after the requested withdrawal the required overcollateralization threshold are still met?
ground_truth:
As regards the first question, in accordance with the general instructions in section 1.7 (
Definition of Encumbrance
) of Annex XVII of the ITS No 451/2021 on asset encumbrance reporting under Article 430 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, it is outlined that an asset shall be treated as encumbered if it has been pledged or if it is subject to any form of arrangement to secure, collateralise or credit enhance any transaction from which it cannot be freely withdrawn. It is noted that assets pledged that are subject to any contractual or regulatory restrictions, or which impact on ratings of bonds in any way in withdrawal, such as for instance assets that by virtue of legal, regulatory or contractual provisions require prior approval before withdrawal or replacement by other assets, should be considered encumbered. In line with this provision, when the release of the asset pledged depends on the prior approval from external parties, the asset should be considered encumbered, in spite of the fact that is an additional collateral on top of collateralization of the covered bond program.
In the section 2.1.1 of Annex XVII of the ITS No 451/2021 related to the specific instructions for retained covered bond, it is stated that in case of retention of part of the issuance, the proposed treatment below shall apply:
(i) where the own covered bonds are not pledged, the amount of the cover pool that is backing those securities retained and not yet pledged shall be reported in the AE-ASS templates as non-encumbered asset;
(ii) where the own covered bonds are pledged, then the amount of the cover pool that is backing those securities retained and pledged shall be included in the AE-ASS template as encumbered assets.
The key point is that the instructions above apply only when the full or in part retention of the covered bond has already taken place, in order to avoid double counting. At the same time, it is not possible to know before the issuance of the covered bond if they will be retained by the bank.
Furthermore, the assets at issue are pledged in a cover pool for a future issuance of covered bonds. Therefore, in spite of the difference in time between the pledge on assets and the issuance of the covered bonds, they still have to be considered encumbered.

dpo.text:
The CRR does not define the term “encumbrance” but refers to it in relation to the calculation of the capital requirements for credit institutions. The definition of encumbrance is provided by the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR). According to Article 4(1)(a) of the CRR, encumbrances include all rights that may affect the value of assets held by a credit institution. In this context, encumbrances can be defined as any right which reduces the value of an asset. This includes, inter alia, any right to receive payment of money or other property, whether arising under contract or otherwise, including any right to set-off against another debt, and any right to withhold payment of money or other property due to the credit institution. Therefore, encumbrances do not only include rights to receive payment of money or other property, but also any right to withhold payment of money or other property due to the credit institution.
In addition, according to Article 4(2) of the CRR, encumbrances shall be valued at their fair market value. Fair market value means the price that would be agreed between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm’s length transaction, taking into account the nature of the encumbrance, its duration and the circumstances surrounding the transaction. For example, a right to withhold payment of money or other property due to the credit institution will have no effect on the value of the asset if the amount withheld is insignificant compared to the total amount due. However, if the amount withheld is significant, the encumbrance will reduce the value of the asset. In such cases, the encumbrance will be valued at the amount withheld.
According to Article 5(6) of the CRR, encumbrances shall be taken into account in calculating the risk-weighted exposure amount of exposures. Credit institutions shall apply the standardised approach to calculate the risk-weighted exposure amount of exposures subject to encumbrances. The risk-weighted exposure amount of an exposure subject to encumbrances shall be calculated using the same formula as for an unencumbered exposure, except that the numerator shall be reduced by the amount of the encumbrance. If the encumbrance is not known, the credit institution shall use the best estimate available. The risk-weighted exposure amount of an exposure subject to encumbrances shall be increased by the amount of the encumbrance if the credit institution has a reasonable expectation that the encumbrance will be released or waived. The increase in the risk-weighted exposure amount shall be applied until the encumbrance is released or waived.
In accordance with Article 5(7) of the CRR, encumbrances shall be included in the calculation of the risk-weighted exposure amount of securitisation positions. The risk-weighted exposure amount of a securitisation position shall be calculated using the same formula as for an unencumbered exposure, except that the numerator shall be reduced by the amount of the encumbrance. If the encumbrance is not known, the credit institution shall use the best estimate available. The risk-weighted exposure amount of a securitisation position shall be increased by the amount of the encumbrance if the credit institution has a reasonable expectation that the encumbrance will be released or waived. The increase in the risk-weighted exposure amount shall be applied until the encumbrance is released or waived.
In summary, encumbrances are any rights that may affect the value of assets held by a credit institution. They are valued at their fair market value and are taken into account in calculating the risk-weighted exposure amount of exposures and securitisation positions.

question: Institutions shall report the total of all other remaining liabilities in section 2; shall we also report weighted average initial maturity and weighted average residual maturity for the remaining liabilities or the average maturities should only be reported for counterparties exceeding a threshold of 1% of total liabilities ? How should we treat received collaterals and the fair value of derivatives, as they don’t fit in any category of product type provided in Annex XXI - Instructions for completing the additional monitoring tools template(UWF, UWNF, REPO, CB, ABS, IGCP) ? And what maturity should we assume for this kind of liabilities ( 1 day, or the initial/ residual maturity of a derivative)?
ground_truth:
Institution shall report weighted average maturities for items to be reported in row 120 “All other liabilities” and columns 070 and 080 of template C 67.00 of Annex XX of final draft implementing technical standard (ITS) on additional liquidity monitoring metrics under Article 415(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (EBA/ITS/2013/11/rev1 (of 24 July 2014)).
For the assessment of initial and residual maturities of no-maturity liabilities as well as on-demand deposits and similar products, see QA 2015_1731.
Derivatives are not to be reported in templates C 67.00 to C 70.00. For the purpose of reporting these templates funding is defined as all financial liabilities other than derivatives and short positions. See QA 2015_2365 for further guidance.
DISCLAIMER:
The present Q&A on Supervisory reporting is provisional. It will be reviewed after the Implementing Regulation is in force and published in the Official Journal, which may differ from the text of the draft ITS to which this Q&A relates.

baseline.text:
The CRR does not specify how to calculate the weighted average initial maturity and weighted average residual maturity for the remaining liabilities. The calculation is left to the discretion of the institution.
The CRR requires institutions to report the total of all other remaining liabilities in section 2. Institutions may choose whether to report the weighted average initial maturity and weighted average residual maturity for the remaining liabilities or the average maturities for each counterparty. If the latter approach is chosen, institutions must provide a description of the method used to determine the average maturities for each counterparty.
The CRR does not require institutions to report the fair value of derivatives and collateral as part of their liquidity coverage ratio. However, if an institution chooses to include these items in its liquidity coverage ratio, it can do so using the same methodology that it uses to measure the fair value of its assets and liabilities under IFRS 7. In particular, the fair value of derivatives and collateral should be calculated based on the market price at the end of the reporting period. For example, if an institution has entered into a repo transaction with a counterparty, the fair value of the repo would be included in the calculation of the liquidity coverage ratio. The fair value of the repo would be determined based on the market price at the end of the reporting period, which could be different from the initial amount of the repo. Similarly, the fair value of a derivative would be determined based on the market price at the end of the reporting period, which could be different from the initial amount of the derivative.
The CRR does not specify a maturity for received collaterals. Therefore, institutions have the flexibility to use the maturity of the underlying asset or the maturity of the collateral itself when calculating the weighted average initial maturity and weighted average residual maturity for the remaining liabilities.

dpo.text:
The CRR does not provide guidance on how to calculate the weighted average initial and residual maturity for the remaining liabilities. The calculation is left to the discretion of the institution.
The CRR requires institutions to report the total of all other remaining liabilities in section 2. Institutions may choose whether to report the weighted average initial maturity and weighted average residual maturity for the remaining liabilities or the average maturities for the remaining liabilities. If the latter option is chosen, the average maturities must be calculated using the same method used for calculating the average maturities for the remaining assets. In case of a mismatch between the two methods, the higher figure must be used.
The CRR does not require institutions to report the average maturities for received collateral and the fair value of derivatives. However, if an institution chooses to report these items, it must do so in accordance with the instructions provided in Annex XXI – Instructions for completing the additional monitoring tools template (UWF, UWNF, REPO, CB, ABS, IGCP).
The CRR does not specify the maturity that should be assumed for received collateral and the fair value of derivatives. Institutions may use their own judgement when determining the appropriate maturity for these items.

question: For exiting the non-performing category Art. 17 no. 157 requires that one year has passed since the forbearance measures were extended. Does that mean that, a) the probation period starts already at the date of the forbearance measure. b) The probation period starts only when the exposure is no longer considered impaired or defaulted.
ground_truth: For the purposes of Art. 17 par. 157 (b) of the draft ITS on Supervisory reporting regarding exit criteria of non-performing exposures with forbearance measures, the one year cure period starts running since the date when the forbearance measures were extended. For the sake of completeness, it should be pointed out that according to Art. 17 par. 176, a minimum 2 year probation period starting as soon as the exposure is considered as "performing", is required in order to exit from the forborne category. Therefore non performing forborne exposures shall stay in the forborne exposure category for at least 3 years (1 year at least in the non-performing forborne exposure category for the cure period stated by Art. 17 par. 157 (b) and 2 years at least in the performing forborne exposure category for the probation period required by Art. 17 par. 176).

question:
Consider a corporate (geographical location DE) exposure guaranteed by a sovereign (geographical location NL).
1) Do the CRM techniques with substitution effect (e.g. guarantees) impact the scoping of relevant exposures for the purposes of the Countercyclical Buffer? E.g. should a corporate exposure with a sovereign guarantee be considered a relevant exposure as sovereign exposures are not considered relevant in accordance with Article 140 of the Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD).
2) If the exposure is considered relevant, should CRM techniques with substitution effects be taken into account for the purposes of the calculation of the capital requirements for the purposes of the determination of the weighted average referred to in Article 140(1) CRD? E.g. can a sovereign guarantee be taken into account in the calculation of the capital requirement for a corporate exposure with a sovereign guarantee?
3) Article 84 of the (draft) ITS 2014/680 Annex 2 (as revised on 8 March 2016) requires geographical allocation on immediate obligor basis, i.e. any CRM (e.g. cross-border guarantee) should not change the geographical location to the location of the CRM provider. The BCBS FAQ on the Basel III Countercyclical Capital Buffer requires the usage of ‘jurisdiction of ultimate risk’, which substitutes the exposure to the location of the CRM provider. Can you please clarify which geographical location should be used for calculation and reporting of the CCyB and template C09.04?
ground_truth:
According to Article 1(4) of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 1152/2014 (RTS on geographical location), in order to determine the geographical location, the exposures are allocated on an immediate obligor basis. Therefore CRM techniques do not change the allocation of an exposure to its geographical location for the purpose of calculation of countercyclical capital buffer.
In this regard:
1)     A corporate exposure is a relevant exposure in accordance with Article 140(4)(a) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD), even if it is partially or fully secured by an eligible guarantee by a government, as the immediate source of risk is not to the sovereign.
2)     The calculation of the capital requirements is based on all applicable provisions of Part Three, Title II of CRR, including those on credit risk mitigation. While the assignment to a country depends solely on the location of the immediate obligor as defined in the RTS on the geographical location, the own funds requirement is calculated taking into account eligible sovereign guarantees and other credit risk mitigants.
3)     For the purposes of reporting template C 09.04 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory Reporting), and as defined in Part II, paragraph
85
84
of the ITS on Supervisory Reporting, the geographical location of of the immediate obligor shall be used.

meta.subject_matter: Calculation of the Countercyclical Capital Buffer

baseline.text:
### Answer

#### 1) Do the CRM techniques with substitution effect (e.g. guarantees) impact the scoping of relevant exposures for the purposes of the Countercyclical Buffer? E.g. should a corporate exposure with a sovereign guarantee be considered a relevant exposure as sovereign exposures are not considered relevant in accordance with Article 140 of the Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD).

The countercyclical buffer is calculated based on the total amount of relevant exposures. Relevant exposures include all exposures that are subject to the standardised approach, IRB exposures and exposures that are subject to the advanced approaches but are not subject to the standardised approach. In addition, exposures that are subject to the standardised approach and IRB exposures that are subject to the advanced approaches may be excluded from the calculation of the countercyclical buffer if they are covered by a credit protection instrument. This exclusion does not apply to exposures that are subject to the standardised approach and IRB exposures that are subject to the advanced approaches and that are covered by a credit protection instrument that has been issued by a third country institution. Therefore, the countercyclical buffer is calculated based on the sum of all relevant exposures, including exposures that are subject to the standardised approach, IRB exposures and exposures that are subject to the advanced approaches but are not subject to the standardised approach. As such, the countercyclical buffer is not impacted by the use of credit protection instruments.

1) No, the countercyclical buffer does not apply to exposures that are guaranteed by a sovereign. This is because the countercyclical buffer applies only to exposures that are subject to the leverage ratio, and sovereign exposures are excluded from the scope of the leverage ratio.

meta.subject_matter: Application of the even deduction rule in case of intragroup transactions booked - by institutions which are parties to the contract - in different amounts

baseline.text:
The even deduction rule is applicable when two or more entities belonging to the same group enter into a contractual arrangement for the purpose of providing financial assistance to one another. The even deduction rule requires that the total amount of the financial assistance provided by all the entities within the group must be equal to the total amount of the financial assistance received from all the other entities within the group. This means that if one entity provides financial assistance to another entity, then the latter entity must provide financial assistance to the former entity in the same amount. If this condition is not met, the financial assistance will be considered as non-performing and will have to be recognised as such under IFRS 9.
In order to determine whether the even deduction rule applies, it is necessary to assess whether the contractual arrangement has been entered into for the purpose of providing financial assistance to one another. In general, the existence of a contractual arrangement between two entities can be inferred from the fact that they have agreed to share losses and/or profits arising from their activities. However, there may be situations where the contractual arrangement does not explicitly state that the parties intend to provide financial assistance to one another but nevertheless meets the requirements of the even deduction rule. For example, if two entities enter into a loan agreement whereby one entity lends money to the other entity at a fixed interest rate, and the repayment terms of the loan are linked to the performance of the borrower, this could be considered as a contractual arrangement for the provision of financial assistance. Similarly, if two entities enter into a guarantee agreement whereby one entity guarantees the payment obligations of the other entity, this could also be considered as a contractual arrangement for the provision of financial assistance.
It should be noted that the even deduction rule only applies to contractual arrangements between entities that belong to the same group. Therefore, if two entities that do not belong to the same group enter into a contractual arrangement for the provision of financial assistance, the even deduction rule will not apply.

dpo.text:
The even deduction rule is applicable when two or more entities belonging to the same group enter into a contractual arrangement for the purpose of providing financial assistance to one another. The even deduction rule requires that the total amount of the financial assistance provided by all the entities within the group must be equal to the total amount of the financial assistance received from all the other entities within the group.
In this context, the term “financial assistance” means any payment made by one entity to another entity within the group, including any guarantee, security, indemnity, credit enhancement, subordination, or similar instrument, as well as any loan, advance, deposit, or other financial accommodation, whether or not secured by collateral, and any other type of financial assistance that may be agreed between the entities within the group. It does not include payments made by one entity to another entity outside the group.
The even deduction rule applies regardless of whether the financial assistance is provided directly or indirectly through third parties. For example, if Entity A provides financial assistance to Entity B, and Entity C provides financial assistance to Entity B, then the total amount of the financial assistance provided by Entities A and C must be equal to the total amount of the financial assistance received by Entities A and C.
The even deduction rule also applies to intra-group transactions that are booked in different amounts by the entities within the group. For example, if Entity A books a financial assistance agreement with Entity B at €1 million, while Entity C books the same financial assistance agreement at €500,000, then the total amount of the financial assistance provided by Entities A and C must be equal to the total amount of the financial assistance received by Entities A and C, i.e., €1.5 million.
It is important to note that the even deduction rule applies only to financial assistance provided by entities within the same group. If an entity provides financial assistance to an entity outside the group, the even deduction rule does not apply. Similarly, if an entity receives financial assistance from an entity outside the group, the even deduction rule does not apply.
The even deduction rule is designed to ensure that the total amount of financial assistance provided by all entities within the group is equal to the total amount of financial assistance received from all other entities within the group. This helps to prevent situations where some entities within the group receive more financial assistance than they provide, leading to imbalances in the group’s financial position.

question: According to Fin-FSA and based on national regulation (Sijoituspalvelulaki 747/2012) the capital conservation buffer should not be applied to investment firms with personnel under 250 and balance sheet amount under 43 million. Validation rule v8714_m requires that this row (CA4_r750) is reported. How should the capital conservation buffer be reported in this case?
ground_truth:
According to article 129 (2) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD), a Member State may exempt small and medium-sized investment firms from the requirements set out in that paragraph if such an exemption does not threaten the stability of the financial system of that Member State.
As notified by the FIN-FSA (Finland national competent authority) to EBA, this exemption has been exercised via the Act on Investment Firms 747/2012, and therefore, VR v8714_m shall not apply to Finnish investment firms classified as SMEs following article 129 (4) of CRD.
VR v8714_m has a “warning” type of severity and will therefore remain as such to allow for the cases described in this Q&A.

question: Can a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II be a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF?
ground_truth:
[ESMA 70-872942901-38 MiFID II MiFIR market structures Q&A, Q&A 5.4]
Yes. Article 53(3) of MiFID II provides that an entity that is not an investment firm or a credit institution can be a member of a regulated market under certain conditions, this rule being extended to MTFs by Article 19(2) of MiFID II.
ESMA considers that this provision should be read in conjunction with the requirements of Article 2(1). Under this provision, a person falling under any of the categories listed in Article 2(1) would not have to be authorised as an investment firm.
However, pursuant to Article 2(1)(d) (ii) of MiFID II, when a person dealing on own account in financial instruments other than commodity derivatives or emission allowances or derivatives thereof and not providing any other investment services or performing any other investment activities in such instruments is also a member of or a participant in a regulated market or an MTF, it falls under the scope of MiFID II, and should accordingly be authorised as an investment firm unless:
it is exempted under points (a), (i) and (j); or
it is a non-financial entity which executes transactions on a trading venue which are objectively measurable as reducing risks directly relating to the commercial activity or treasury financing activity of that non-financial entity or its group.
As a consequence, the reference in Article 53(3) to persons other than investment firms and credit institutions only relates to entities that are exempted from authorisation under Article 2(1), such as insurance companies or collective investment undertakings, as long as their own regulatory framework permits them to do so.
This Q&A does not address the issue of non-EEA firms being a member or participant of an EEA trading venue.

meta.legal_act: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II) Directive 2014/65/EU- Secondary Markets
meta.subject_matter: Unauthorised person as an investment firm meeting the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II being a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF

baseline.text:
The answer to this question can be found in the EBA’s Q&As on the subject matter of “Unauthorised persons as investment firms meeting the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II”:

1. Can a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II be a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF?
Yes, such a person may be a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF if it meets all other conditions for membership or participation set out in the relevant legislation.
2. Does a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II need to be registered as a credit institution or investment firm under the CRR or AIFMD respectively?
No, such a person does not need to be registered as a credit institution or investment firm under the CRR or AIFMD respectively.
3. If a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II becomes authorised as an investment firm, will it lose its status as a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF?
No, once a person has been authorised as an investment firm, it cannot cease to be a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF unless it ceases to meet the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II.
4. What are the consequences of a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II becoming authorised as an investment firm?
If a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II becomes authorised as an investment firm, it must comply with the provisions of MiFID II applicable to investment firms, including those relating to the authorisation process, the obligation to notify the competent authority of any changes to its business activities, the requirement to maintain adequate organisational and administrative arrangements, and the prohibition on engaging in certain activities without prior authorisation.
5. Is there a distinction between a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II and a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 54(3) of MiFID II?

question: For application of the grandfathering rules defined in Article 484 CRR and following, does the change in debtor resulting from a merger means that a new capital instrument has been issued and that its eligibility for grandfathering or for full eligibility as an own fund instrument should be assessed at the date of the merger or should one use the initial characteristics of the bond?
ground_truth:
As specified in
Q&A 2013_16
, changes made to pre-CRR instruments shall aim at ensuring a full eligibility under the provisions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 but shall not aim at allowing a grandfathering of the instrument. For the case at hand, a change of the debtor or the legal format shall not per se be regarded as a material change and does not necessarily lead to the requalification as a new instrument.
According to Article 484(2) CRR, the provisions of Article 484 CRR regarding the eligibility for grandfathering of own funds instruments apply to the instrument of Bank 2 from 1 January 2014, provided that the instrument qualified as own funds under the national transposition measures for Directive 2006/48/EC on 31 December 2011.
The prevailing swap rates and credit margins on the merger date are not relevant to assess the eligibility for grandfathering or the compliance with the CRR criteria on own funds instruments.

meta.subject_matter: Grandfathering of own funds instruments

baseline.text: The grandfathering rules apply to all existing debt instruments, including those which have been issued before the entry into force of the CRR. The grandfathering rules do not distinguish between different types of debt instruments. Therefore, the change in debtor resulting from a merger does not mean that a new capital instrument has been issued and that its eligibility for grandfathering or for full eligibility as an own funds instrument should be assessed at the date of the merger.

dpo.text: The grandfathering rules apply to all existing debt instruments which were outstanding on 1 January 2014. The grandfathering rules do not apply to any subsequent changes in the characteristics of these debt instruments. Therefore, if there is a change in the characteristics of a debt instrument after 1 January 2014, it will no longer qualify for grandfathering.

The question refers to the implementation of the Financial Conglomerates Directive (FiCD), which requires financial conglomerates to report consolidated data to competent authorities. The Consolidated Reporting Framework (CRF) provides the methodology for this reporting. The CRF includes templates for various types of information, including risk concentration. The question asks whether the CRF allows reporting exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies. The CRF does not explicitly address this issue. However, it can be inferred from the CRF's instructions that the reporting of exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies is allowed.

To understand why this is the case, we need to look at the underlying legislation. The Financial Conglomerates Directive (FiCD) requires financial conglomerates to report consolidated data to competent authorities. The Consolidated Reporting Framework (CRF) provides the methodology for this reporting. The CRF includes templates for various types of information, including risk concentration. One such template is the "FC.06 Template - Risk Concentration - Exposure by Counterparties". The CRF instructions state that the template should include "the exposure amount, the maturity date, the currency, and the type of instrument". This suggests that the CRF allows reporting exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies.

However, the CRF does not provide any guidance on how to handle situations where exposures to the same counterparty are denominated in different currencies. In these cases, the CRF requires reporting a single exposure amount for the counterparty, regardless of the number of currencies involved. This approach may lead to some confusion, as it may not accurately reflect the true nature of the exposures.

To resolve this issue, the European Banking Authority (EBA) has issued a Technical Standards (TS) document that provides more detailed guidance on the reporting of exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies. According to the TS, when reporting exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies, the CRF requires reporting a single exposure amount for the counterparty, calculated using the average exchange rate over the reporting period. This approach ensures that the reported exposure amount reflects the true economic impact of the exposures to the counterparty, regardless of the number of currencies involved.

In conclusion, while the CRF does not explicitly allow reporting exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies, it can be inferred from its instructions that this is permitted. The EBA's TS provides further guidance on how to handle these situations, recommending reporting a single exposure amount for the counterparty, calculated using the average exchange rate over the reporting period.

### Answer
The question refers to the implementation of the Financial Conglomerates Directive (FiCD), which requires financial conglomerates to report their exposure to other financial institutions (FI) and non-FI counterparties. The question concerns the reporting of exposures to FI counterparties in the Financial Conglomerates Reporting Template (FCRT).

The Financial Conglomerates Reporting Template (FCRT) is a standardised template developed by the European Banking Authority (EBA). It is used by financial conglomerates to report their exposure to FIs and non-FIs to national competent authorities (NCAs) under the FiCD. The FCRT includes several sections, one of which is "Risk concentration - Exposure by counterparties". In this section, financial conglomerates are required to report the total amount of exposures they hold towards each FI and non-FI counterparty.

The question asks whether it is possible to report the exposures towards the same FI counterparty in different currencies in the FCRT. The question also asks how to report the exposures towards the same FI counterparty when the exposures are denominated in different currencies.

To answer these questions, we need to refer to the relevant provisions of the FiCD and the implementing legislation.

The FiCD requires financial conglomerates to report their exposure to FIs and non-FIs in the FCRT. The FCRT is based on the Data Point Methodology (DPM) 3.5, which provides detailed instructions on how to calculate and report the exposure to FIs and non-FIs. According to DPM 3.5, the exposure to an FI counterparty should be calculated using the notional amount of the transaction multiplied by the risk weight assigned to the counterparty. The risk weight is determined based on the credit quality of the counterparty and the type of transaction. For example, if the counterparty is a bank, the risk weight would be 20% for retail exposures and 50% for wholesale exposures.

However, the question mentions that the exposures towards the same FI counterparty may be denominated in different currencies. This means that the notional amounts of the transactions will vary depending on the currency in which they are denominated. Therefore, the question raises the issue of how to aggregate the exposures towards the same FI counterparty in different currencies in the FCRT.

In response to this question, we can refer to the implementing legislation, namely the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2454 of 14 December 2022, which specifies the format and content of the FCRT. According to Article 6(1)(a) of this regulation, the FCRT should include a table called "Template FC.06 - Risk concentration - Exposure by counterparties". This table contains two columns: "Counterparty identifier" and "Exposure". The "Counterparty identifier" column should contain the identification code of the counterparty, while the "Exposure" column should contain the aggregated exposure to the counterparty, including all exposures denominated in different currencies.

Therefore, according to the implementing legislation, the exposures towards the same FI counterparty in different currencies should be aggregated in the "Exposure" column of the "Template FC.06 - Risk concentration - Exposure by counterparties" table. This aggregation should be done based on the notional amounts of the transactions, taking into account the risk weights assigned to the counterparty and the currency denomination of the transactions.

In conclusion, the exposures towards the same FI counterparty in different currencies should be reported in the "Exposure" column of the "Template FC.06 - Risk concentration - Exposure by counterparties" table, aggregating the notional amounts of the transactions, taking into account the risk weights assigned to the counterparty and the currency denomination of the transactions.

question: Is the exemption of applying strong customer authentication, in respect of legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions through the use of dedicated payment processes or protocols that are only made available to payers who are not consumers applicable to both payment initiation and account information services? Or, is it solely applicable to payment initiation service?
ground_truth:
Article 17 of the
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389
states that payment service providers may decide not to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) “in respect of legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions through the use of dedicated payment processes or protocols that are only made available to payers who are not consumers”, provided competent authorities are satisfied that the levels of security are equivalent to those provided for by Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2). This exemption applies solely to payment initiation, given it refers to “legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions”; it does not apply to account information.
Payment initiation as a process is not to be confused with payment initiation services, with the latter referring to a payment that is initiated by a third party.

question: Paragraphs 40) and 41) of the Guidelines on performance fees recommend that the length of the performance reference period  (if this is shorter than the whole life of the fund) should be set equal to at least 5 years. How should the performance reference period be set for the first time in light of the application date of the guidelines?
ground_truth:
[ESMA 34-43-392 UCITS Q&A, Section 11, 2a] & [ESMA 34-32-352 AIFMD Q&A, Section 15, 2]
Managers of any funds already compliant with paragraphs 40)
[1]
and 41)
[2]
of the Guidelines on performance fees before the application date of the guidelines should look at the past 5 years/whole life of the fund for the purpose of setting the performance reference period
[3]
(i.e. they should not reset the performance reference period after the application date of the guidelines).
In all the other cases, managers should apply the performance reference period starting from the beginning of the financial year following 6 months from the application date of the Guidelines (i.e. the performance reference period should start at the beginning of the financial year following 5 July 2021; by way of example, if the financial year of the fund starts on 1 September 2021, the period 1 September 2021 – 1 September 2022 should be considered as the first year of the performance reference period).
[1]
Paragraph 40) of the Guidelines on performance fees states that “In case the fund employs a performance fee model based on a benchmark index, it should be ensured that any underperformance of the fund compared to the benchmark is clawed back before any performance fee becomes payable. To this purpose, the length of the performance reference period, if this is shorter than the whole life of the fund, should be set equal to at least 5 years.”
[2]
Paragraph 41) of the Guidelines on performance fees states that “Where a fund utilises a HWM model, a performance fee should be payable only where, during the performance reference period, the new HWM exceeds the last HWM. The starting point to be considered in the calculations should be the initial offering price per share. For the HWM model, in case the performance reference period is shorter than the whole life of the fund, the performance reference period should be set equal to at least five years on a rolling basis. In this case, performance fee may only be claimed if the outperformance exceeds any underperformances during the previous five years and performance fees should not crystallise more than once a year”.
[3]
This is defined as “the time horizon over which the performance is measured and compared with that of the reference indicator, at the end of which the mechanism for the compensation for past underperformance (or negative performance) can be reset”.

question: Should the ECL on debt instruments classified at fair value through OCI under IFRS9 be included within the calculation of the amount to be added back to CET1 as set in Article 473a.2 ( “static approach”)?
ground_truth:
Article 473a of the Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 establishes that, under the “static approach”, institutions are required to calculate the difference between the expected credit losses determined in accordance with paragraphs 5.5.5 and 5.5.3 of IFRS 9 at the implementation date (Article 473a(2)(b)(i)) and the amount of impairment losses determined in accordance with paragraphs 63,64, 65, 67, 68 and 70 of IAS 39 determined at 31 December 2017 or the day before the initial application of IFRS 9 (Article 473a(2)(b)(ii)). The resulting amount is the one to be considered for the application of the transitional arrangements.
The same logic, with the exclusion of credit-impaired instruments, is valid for the “dynamic approach” as established in paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 473a.
This being said, it is important to note that Article 473a does not distinguish expected credit losses recognised for instruments measured at amortised cost from expected credit losses recognised for instruments measured at fair value through other comprehensive income - FVOCI. For this reason, impairment losses on debt instruments classified as FVOCI should, therefore, be included in the calculation required by Article 473a as suggested in the alternative 1 presented by the submitter.
In addition, following the amendments introduced to Article 468 CRR, please note that the treatment of impairment losses recognised on exposures to central governments, regional governments, local authorities or public sector entities measured at FVOCI should follow the specifications under
Q&A 5346
.

question:
What is the treatment of a securities lending and borrowing service with regard to the LCR?
***
FR:
Quel est le traitement accordé au ratio de couverture des besoins de liquidité pour un service de prêt et d’emprunt de titres?
ground_truth:
The situation described includes two distinct transactions (lender to organisation, organization to borrower) that have to be treated separately.
From the perspective of the securities lender:
The transaction between the securities lender and the organisation is understood as being an unsecured securities lending transaction.
For the securities lender, assets lent under a securities lending and borrowing service do not meet the relevant general and operational requirements to qualify as HQLA in accordance with Articles 7 and 8 of the Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61. Specifically, the three day recall period is an impediment to the securities lender having ready access to its holdings of liquid assets at any time during the 30 calendar day period.
The securities lender may consider an inflow of the liquidity value corresponding to the securities lent if they are eligible to the stock of liquid assets (after being returned to the securities lender) and if the conditions of Article 32(1) are met (i.e. if they have been contractually recalled to be recovered no later than 3 business days or are contractually due within the next 30 calendar days).
From the perspective of the securities borrower:
For the securities borrower, the transaction shall be treated as a collateral swap since collateral has been provided and placed at the organisation's disposal. The securities borrowed may be included in the liquidity buffer if they meet the general and operational requirements to qualify as HQLA in accordance with Articles 7 and 8 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61.
For the calculation of cash flows, two different situations may arise and are subject to differing treatments:
Where the
liquidity value of the
securities borrowed
exceeds the liquidity value of the collateral provided
are subject to a lower haircut under Chapter 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61 than the collateral provided
, the option for the securities lender to recall its securities shall be assumed to be exercised and the securities borrower shall report an outflow
corresponding to the excess liquidity value
in accordance with Article 28(4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61.

meta.subject_matter: Treatment of a securities lending and borrowing service with regard to the LCR / Traitement d’un service de prêt et d’emprunt de titres en ce qui concerne le ratio de couverture des besoins de liquidité

baseline.text:
The CRR does not define what constitutes a securities lending and borrowing service. The definition of this type of activity is provided by the Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/35 amending Directive 2009/138/EC as regards the liquidity coverage requirement (LCR). This definition is based on the definition of the term “securities financing” in Article 4(1)(a) of the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR).

The CRR defines a securities financing as any transaction that involves the transfer of ownership of a security from one party to another for a period of time, which may be temporary or permanent, in return for cash or other assets. A securities lending and borrowing service is defined as a business activity where a counterparty provides a borrower with a security and receives cash or other assets in return. In addition, the counterparty must have the right to repossess the security at any time during the agreed period of time. The counterparty also has the obligation to return the cash or other assets received in exchange for the security to the borrower when the latter requests it. The counterparty can only retain the cash or other assets if the borrower fails to repay the loan within the agreed period of time.

dpo.text:
The CRR does not define what constitutes a securities lending and borrowing service. The definition of this type of activity is provided by the Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/35 amending Directive 2009/138/EC as regards the liquidity coverage requirement (LCR). This definition is based on the definition of the term “securities lending and borrowing” used in the Basel Committee’s Guidelines for Securities Lending and Borrowing published in June 2010.
The LCR applies to all institutions that have a significant amount of assets consisting of securities. It requires these institutions to hold sufficient high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to cover their net cash outflows over a 30-day period under stress conditions. In order to determine whether a given asset qualifies as HQLA, it must meet certain criteria set out in the CRR. These include the maturity profile, the ability to be converted into cash within 10 business days, and the absence of restrictions on its sale or transfer. A securities lending and borrowing service meets these criteria if it complies with the requirements laid down in the Delegated Directive.

question: In EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 73 it is explained that in the calculation of the one-year default rates the number of obligors is used. Is it always mandatory to count one legal entity as one obligor, or can a group of legal entities for which there is no difference in risk due to an appropriate guarantee (i.e. those will default together) be counted as one obligor?
ground_truth:
According to Article 172(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2019/876 (CRR2), each separate legal entity to which the institution is exposed shall be separately rated. As such, the existence of a group of connected clients defined in Article 4(1)(39) CRR or the existence of third-party rating support as described in paragraph 62 of the Guidelines on PD estimation, LGD estimation and the treatment of defaulted exposures (EBA/GL/2017/16) is instead to be considered in the assignment of these separate obligors to rating grades or pools. As a matter of fact, the mere existence of an ‘appropriate guarantee’ or the existence of a rating transfer does not necessarily imply that the obligor and the third party represent a single risk with only joint defaults possible. In particular, the default status should be assessed according to the internal policies of the institution, as specified in paragraph 61 of said Guidelines, and is not necessarily automatic.
According to Article 180(1)(a) and Article 180(2)(a) CRR, institutions shall estimate PDs by obligor grade from long-run averages of one-year default rates. On this regard, Chapter 5.3 of the above mentioned Guidelines clarify the CRR requirements for the purpose of calibrating PD estimates. More in detail, for the purpose of calculating the one-year default rate referred to in Article 4(1) (78) of the CRR, paragraph 73 of the GL clarifies that the denominator “consists of the number of non-defaulted obligors with any credit obligation observed at the beginning of the one-year observation period”.
It follows that, irrespective of “the treatment of individual obligor clients and groups of connected clients” for the purpose of assigning an exposure to obligor grades or pools in accordance with Article 172(1) (d) of the CRR, each separate legal entity to which the institution is exposed constitutes an obligor for the purpose of calibrating PD estimates to the “long-run averages of one-year default rates” as defined in Article 4(1)(78) CRR.
However, where there is a significant proportion of connected obligors with a high default correlation within a considered PD model, institutions should analyse the level of risk of such obligors compared with other obligors in that model and, where necessary, reflect the difference in the level of risk in the model through appropriate risk drivers and rating criteria, for instance through different calibration segments.
In that case of high default correlation of connected obligors institutions should ensure that the lack of independence of defaults does not lead to biased results or wrong conclusions during the development or the validation of the PD model where one year default rates are computed, in particular if this high default correlation of connected obligors in the model implies a violation of the assumptions required by the underlying statistical methodologies (e.g. in the validation of model performance) in accordance with article 180(1)(d).
Please note that the differences in the treatment of unfunded credit protection and rating transfer are further clarified in
Q&A 4598
.

meta.subject_matter: Calculation of the number of obligors

baseline.text: The CRR does not provide any guidance on this matter. The EBA has published a Q&A document on this topic, but it only provides some examples of how to calculate the number of obligors. In particular, the EBA states that “the number of obligors should reflect the number of distinct counterparties” (EBA/GL/2017/16, para 73). This means that if two legal entities have the same credit risk profile, they may be considered as one obligor. However, the EBA also notes that “in practice, it might be difficult to determine whether two legal entities have the same credit risk profile” (ibid.). Therefore, the EBA recommends that banks use their own judgement when determining whether two legal entities should be treated as one obligor.

dpo.text:
The CRR does not provide any guidance on how to determine whether two or more legal entities should be treated as one obligor. The EBA has published a Q&A document on this topic, which provides some examples of situations where it would be appropriate to treat two or more legal entities as one obligor. In particular, the EBA states that:

• Two or more legal entities may be considered as one obligor if they have a common parent company, or if they are part of a group of companies that share the same business model and are subject to similar credit risk.
• Two or more legal entities may also be considered as one obligor if they are legally separate but are under common control by a single person or entity, such as a bank holding company, or if they are subsidiaries of a single parent company.
• Two or more legal entities may also be considered as one obligor if they are legally independent but are closely linked through contractual arrangements, such as guarantees, collateral agreements, or other forms of contingent liabilities.

It is up to each institution to decide whether these criteria apply to its own situation. If so, then the institution must use the number of obligors equal to the number of legal entities that meet these criteria. Otherwise, the institution must use the number of obligors equal to the total number of legal entities.
